CausalChain: Gut microbiome dysbiosis -> altered production of microbial metabolites (e.g., butyrate) -> modification of hepatic epigenetic landscape -> differential methylation of AFP gene promoter -> increased expression of AFP-L3 isoform -> potential for early HCC detection
Hypothesis: Dysbiosis of the gut microbiome induces epigenetic modifications in hepatocytes that favour the production of the AFP-L3 isoform, thus serving as an early biomarker for HCC when combined with specific gut microbial metabolite profiles.
Abstract: This hypothesis proposes that alterations in the gut microbiome can induce epigenetic changes in the liver, specifically affecting the methylation status of the AFP gene promoter. Such changes may lead to an early preferential production of the AFP-L3 isoform even before overt tumor growth is detectable by conventional imaging. By integrating serum AFP-L3 levels with profiling of gut microbiome‐derived metabolites, notably short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, it may be possible to establish a more sensitive early detection tool for hepatocellular carcinoma. This approach could also elucidate mechanistic links between dysbiosis, liver inflammation, and the oncogenic process in HCC.
